comment.value:
(a) Summary

This paper introduces LibriBrain, a 50+ hour within-subject MEG dataset for naturalistic speech listening, the largest of its kind. It includes detailed annotations, standardized splits, baselines, and a Python library to ensure reproducibility.

(b) Strengths: 

This 50+ hours dataset enables modeling directions not previously possible with non-invasive brain data. Accessibility through Hugging Face, pip-installable loaders, and reproducible baselines make it especially valuable for ML researchers. The release sets a high standard for usability in neuroimaging datasets.

(c) Weaknesses: 

The dataset is limited to a single subject, which restricts generalizability. Benchmarks are preliminary, with small test sets and simple baselines. Metadata and BIDS compliance are incomplete, and methodological details (e.g., split leakage, statistical corrections) remain potential issues.

(d) Reasons for Acceptance: 

Despite the above limitations in (c), the scale, quality, and accessibility of the dataset represent a significant contribution to the D&B community. All reviewers recommended acceptance, highlighting its likely impact and broad interest.

(e) Rebuttal & Discussion: 

Authors clarified downsampling, explained evaluation metrics, and justified staged BIDS release. They also acknowledged future work on multi-subject data and stronger baselines. Reviewers maintained positive scores, agreeing that the dataset’s contribution outweighs remaining concerns.

I thank the authors for their response.

As noted in my review, the authors present and publicly release what appears to be the largest naturalistic single-subject MEG dataset to date. This dataset offers promising opportunities for advancing BCI models and improving our understanding of within-subject modeling—an important and timely contribution. While some of my concerns were not fully addressed in the rebuttal, I still believe that the manuscript—describing the dataset created for the PNLP Challenge—serves as a helpful vehicle to promote its adoption and use by the ML community.

That said, if the dataset was primarily prepared in the context of a specific challenge, it would help to clarify this framing within the manuscript. As it stands, the current presentation suggests a general-purpose dataset release, and I had assumed the authors had undertaken additional efforts to provide a complete dataset for broader use. I share reviewer MkVo’s view that the current narrative could be strengthened, though I don’t see this as a major issue for a dataset-track submission—especially one that is already generating interest within the community.

Finally, given that the dataset is introduced as "LibriBrain comes with a Python library for streamlined integration with deep learning frameworks," I think it is important to provide at least minimal testing and documentation of the testing environment. While I understand that more comprehensive testing may be planned for future versions, including a basic, reproducible test setup in this release would significantly improve usability for others in the community.

rebuttal.value:
We greatly appreciate the reviewer's in-depth analysis and helpful comments.

**In regards to the comment about the model performance tables showing accuracy against random baseline and does not seem particularly informative:**

Thank you for the very thoughtful feedback. We would like to highlight that the tables with the models results and comparison to random baseline, are not meant to show the performance of an optimized model. Rather, we use the model performance to indicate that the data contained the signal required for training a model on these tasks. In a NeurIPS competition launched for this data (PNPL LibriBrain Competition - Landau et al. 2025)  we already have SOTA results that far exceed the reference baseline. In this case the improvement over random baseline is only an indication of a signal in the data and it is driven by both the data quality and its size (smaller subset will yield lower performance). The supplemental material on the benefit of repeated stimuli can indeed be used to detect the relevant signal in the data, but as practitioners in the field it has been our experience that the most reliable way to assess the quality of a dataset is to check how it fairs when using it for training models.


**In regards to the feedback and question about day-to-day drift of the MEG signals over the long time period of data collection:**

We thank the reviewer for raising an interesting point about potential day-to-day drift in the MEG signal across recording sessions (that were spanning multiple months in total). To some extent, we expect to see some test-retest variability but overall we expect neural responses to be stable over time. To investigate this, we measured amplitude, phase and power modulations associated with speech and non-speech segments. See Figure 9 in the Appendix for a similar analysis which targets low frequency neural responses evoked by the presence vs. absence of the auditory stimulus. We ran this analysis for each chapter separately and we found that there is some variability across sessions possibly due to small differences in signal and noise, however the mean and the standard deviation remains similar across all chapters from book 1-7.

**In regards to the comment about the clear runway for scaling and lager data collection in a single participant setup:**

What is the outlook on single-subject scaling for the field? This is a good question. For surgical recordings, it is very difficult in practice to scale data within the same subject. By contrast, non-invasive scans can be repeated with relative ease in healthy volunteers. We are currently collecting many times the data represented in the LibriBrain dataset – including from the same subject. It is not outside the realm of possibility that we will collect an order of magnitude more data for the same subject within the coming years. In parallel, PNPL has been making progress in effectively leveraging data from multiple subjects across multiple studies (see e.g. Jayalath et al. 2025). So far, the performance gains have been slower by combining subjects and datasets than by continuing to collect data from a small number of subjects (e.g. one here). But a key question we are asking ourselves in the group is whether this will remain the case as the community continues to innovate new methods. Whatever the outcome, we will try to focus our time and other resources on the problems that we think will help move the field forward the most.

**In regards to the request for a deeper view of the neural data in Figure 1:**

In Figure 1, we chose to show a few single-channel time series as representative examples of MEG signals rather than using a matrix representation (e.g., channels x time) because time series plots more clearly convey key aspects of data quality and structure that are critical to assess neurophysiological recordings. Specifically, they allow readers to directly observe the temporal dynamics of the signal, including characteristic spectral profiles, trial structure, and potential artifacts. While matrix representations may appear more compact, they often obscure meaningful frequency information and make it difficult to assess rapidly evolving temporal patterns. Moreover, highly transient spatial patterns across MEG sensors are not easily interpretable in a matrix format even if a reference topographic map is provided (such as the sensor layout in Figure 1A). In contrast, single-channel time series examples give a more intuitive sense of signal clarity, variability, and artifact contamination, making them a more effective way to demonstrate recording quality, especially for readers less familiar with MEG sensor geometry and neuroanatomy. This approach is also consistent with common data visualization conventions in the field of neurophysiology, where time series plots are typically used to illustrate the quality and structure of electrophysiological signals such as MEG, EEG, and LFP. In addition, we would like to clarify that in Figure 1B only the first row of the matrix is showing audio recordings (i.e. mel spectrogram) while the second, third, fourth and final rows are showing MEG recordings measured from different sensors (i.e. MEG 1, MEG 2, MEG 3, MEG 306). There is no statistical test. The different colors are only meant to visualize phonemes annotations (according with the color-coding scheme represented in Figure 1D-E).

**In regards to the feedback about possible comparison between inter-subject and intra-subject scaling:**

For a future release, we are collecting data from many more subjects while keeping the task and scanner constant. We believe we will be in a better position then to provide this analysis. 

Insofar as this can be surmised by comparing different datasets, prior work has shown that the greatest improvements in neural decoding come from scaling up data within-subject (e.g. d’Ascoli et al. 2024). For example, d’Ascoli et al. show that Armeni et al. dataset consistently outperforms the Schoffelen et al. dataset on a word classification task, even though the latter is about 3x as big (106 total hours in Schoffelen et al. compared to 30 total hours in Armeni et al.). It turns out that the key difference is that Armeni et al. provide more data per subject (10 hours per subject compared to 1.1 hours per subject in Schoffelen et al.). 

This came up in reply to another reviewer, so apologies for repeating some of the same text here. This is clearly emerging as an interesting question for the community.

**In regards to unclarity about the Figure 3 comparison of LibriBrain to Armeni on “Word Classification” task.**

Thank you for highlighting this confusing aspect of this comparison plot. As you correctly pointed out Armeni contain approximately 30 hours of collected data but we were able to compare side by side with the LibriBrain dataset because the “Word Classification” model is trained by using **overlapping** MEG segments. So even though the samples are not unique, the plot still represent a fair comparison in regards to the training strategy applied for both datasets. As for the performance difference between LibriBrain and Armeni - although we have not carried out in-depth analysis to understand the root of this performance gap, we believe part of it can be attributed to the increased variety of in-subject data collected for LibriBrain.

**In regards to the issue of a single-subject nature of the dataset will limit its usability:**

Prior work has shown that the greatest improvements in neural decoding come from scaling up data within-subject (e.g. d’Ascoli et al. 2024). It turns out that the key difference is that Armeni et al. provide more data per subject (10 hours per subject compared to 1.1 hours per subject in Schoffelen et al.). To drive progress in neural decoding, we have therefore focused first on scaling up the amount of data per subject to >50 hours. That said, we hope the reviewer will be pleased to hear that we are currently working on data for a future release which will include more subjects. Please watch this space.

**In regards to not focusing on the impact of scaling models by leveraging more data:**

We also agree very much on the importance of scaling models and not just data – we are currently working on this as a separate project.


**In regards to concerns about potential ethical issues involving experimentation with human participants:**

We appreciate the reviewer’s comment about potential ethical issues involving experimentation with human participants. In the current version of the manuscript, we briefly mentioned how we took care of potential ethical issues we believe that these should be addressed in the paper (see Appendix, “B. Data Collection Methods”). First, the study was approved by the University of Oxford Medical Sciences Interdivisional Research Ethics Committee (R90053/RE002). The Ethical Committee operates in accordance with national regulations and international standards for research involving human participants. Specifically, the committee’s procedures are guided by the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki, ensuring that participants’ rights, safety, and well-being are prioritized throughout the study. Second, prior to participation, volunteers provided informed consent authorising the use of pseudonymised data for research purposes. Finally, we would also point to appendix A.1 (“Ethical Considerations”) for a broader discussion. If there are any lingering questions, we would be very happy to discuss this further.

We appreciate the reviewer's in-depth analysis and comments.

**In regards to the issue of the data not being BIDS compliant:**

The data should be “consistent” with BIDS standards, if not yet “complete” or indeed “compliant”. The key is that each book is a BIDS dataset (e.g. `Sherlock1`, `Sherlock2`, etc.) and all of these are collected together within `LibriBrain`. In other words, LibriBrain was designed to be a collection of BIDS datasets. For now, we’re mainly using the `derivatives` subdirectories within each BIDS dataset for the serialised data. What’s currently missing in the current release is the `sub` subdirectory for each book. In practice, the other standard files (e.g. `dataset_description.json`, `participants.json`, `participants.tsv`, and `README`) can be left underspecified so are not always informative. Nonetheless, these will be added after the associated "LibriBrain" PNPL Competition (Landau et al. 2025) and will not require deleting anything downloaded from the Hugging Face repo. 

One reason for not releasing the BIDS data for the competition is that we were concerned that the memory footprint of the dataset could become an obstacle. We note that the BIDS version takes up many times more storage as the serialised version (i.e. multiple hundreds of GB vs about 50 GB). We also did not want domain expertise to discourage participants without neuroscience backgrounds. For example, we did not want the competition to become all about preprocessing. By releasing serialised data, the data can be thought of as “just” tensors for machine learning. Nonetheless, once the competition finishes, we will release the “raw” data and complete the BIDS format.


**In regards to the concerns about limited metadata in the current version:**

We collected vertical and horizontal electrooculograms (EOG) to monitor eye blinks and eye movements, electrocardiogram (ECG) to keep track of cardiac activity and electromyogram (EMG) to detect potential articulatory movements. For each of these, we provided a detailed description in the Appendix (see “B.3 Data Acquisition”). The first dataset release was designed to better suit the requirements of the participants in the PNPL Competition (Landau et al. 2025), for which we aimed to be as inclusive as possible. Specifically, considering that most of the competition participants will have domain general engineering background (AI, machine learning), we wanted to make it easy to join the competition such that domain specific expertise about neural signal processing is not required. The rationale for not including the metadata was to focus on model architecture and hyperparameter tuning rather than pre-processing. Nevertheless, we are planning to provide comprehensive access to all the metadata in a future BIDS compliant release that will be available after the end of the PNPL Competition. In the present release, linguistic annotations (speech/non-speech, words, phonemes) are already available in .tsv event files (for a detailed description see “B.5 Annotations/Event Files” in the Appendix).

**In regards to the lack of documentation on PNPL library usage, data directory structure and Python version support:**

We’re sorry that you experienced issues that prevented you from using the dataset using the PNPL package. While the library ships with an integrated download functionality that automatically downloads the dataset from HuggingFace into the correct folder structure, we hear what you're saying about documenting and supporting use cases that don’t wish to rely on it. For the next release of the library, we have added more comprehensive documentation to the codebase to address the issue. Thank you for flagging this for us.

Similarly, while we have not experienced issues with Python versions from 3.9 onwards (the oldest still supported release), we have not done extensive testing, nor have we documented our testing environment. Both will be addressed in future versions. Thank you again for raising these issues.

We greatly appreciate the reviewer’s in-depth analysis and comments.

**In regards to the concerns of linguistic context leaking due to to all splits taken from a contiguous story read by the same narrator:**

We spent a lot of time reflecting on potential information leakage between the training, validation, and test splits. For example, we took the rather extreme action of recording the training data on different days than the validation and test data – as a strong protection against “nonsense correlations in neuroscience” (Harris 2020). In using different parts of the same audiobook for all data splits, we have followed other influential datasets in this space such as Armeni et al. 2022. 


**In regards to the choice to downsample the data from 1 kHz to 250 Hz:**

Downsampling MEG data is also common across the field (see e.g. Défossez et al. 2023, d'Ascoli et al. 2024, Jayalath et al. 2025). There are a few reasons for this. One is that it reduces file sizes and improves computational efficiency while focusing on significant frequency ranges in the brain – neural oscillations divide into named frequency bands such as delta (0.1–4 Hz), theta (4–8 Hz), alpha (8–12 Hz), beta (12–30 Hz), gamma (30–70 Hz), and high-gamma (70–130 Hz). 

This is what we mean when we write in the paper that: “The recordings were originally sampled at 1 kHz but were downsampled during preprocessing to 250 Hz to preserve oscillations into the high-gamma range (70–125 Hz).”

As detailed in the paper (e.g. in section B.4), the data were bandpass filtered between 0.1 and 125 Hz. We subsequently downsampled the data to twice the maximum frequency (125 Hz x 2) to respect the Nyquist theorem. This is how we arrived at the downsampling rate of 250 Hz (which also evenly divides the original 1,000 Hz sample rate). 

A second reason to downsample the data is that our head-positioning system uses frequencies around 300 Hz. If we did not downsample the data below this, then the neural data would include this high-frequency noise. 


**In regards to the issue of the statistical reporting that doesn’t account for multiple comparisons across the many metrics and seeds:**

We appreciate the reviewer’s comment regarding potential corrections for multiple comparisons. In the manuscript, we report multiple performance metrics (e.g., F1-macro, balanced accuracy, ROC AUC, Jaccard index, and cross-entropy loss) to provide a comprehensive benchmarking for future studies which will compare their performance against this baseline. The idea is that if one other study uses balanced accuracy but another uses ROC AUC, then the reader could compare the results in our paper against each (since we list results both in terms of balanced accuracy and ROC AUC). 

In other words, these metrics are not used for independent hypothesis testing, but rather serve as descriptive performance indicators. We are not conducting multiple statistical tests per metric, nor are we performing model selection based on multiple testing across seeds. Our aim is to present a transparent and multi-faceted evaluation, rather than to claim statistical significance for individual metrics


**In regards to the concerns raised about benchmarks, the validation and test sets size, simple model, and limited number of recognition tasks:**

Whether the val/test splits are appropriately sized would seem to depend on the task. For example, speech detection provides a label for every sample (250 per second). While there are benefits to standardized data splits, the data loader that comes with the dataset makes it easy for the user to define custom data splits. So more data can be easily allocated to custom val/test splits, if desired.

We agree with the reviewer that the current recognition tasks—speech detection, phoneme classification, and word classification—only partially capture the full complexity of the dataset. That said, these three tasks were selected as illustrations and are not meant to be exhaustive. As a starting point, we aimed to design decoding tasks that tap into largely non-overlapping neural and linguistic features of speech perception. In particular, the speech detection task is more concerned with detecting synchronization vs. absence of synchronization with the auditory input during speech and non-speech segments, respectively. The phoneme classification task is designed to capture lower-level motor and acoustic features associated with the most basic speech unit (the phoneme). The word classification task involves higher-level semantic and syntactic features. Because words encapsulate conceptual and syntactic information, this task is designed to engage distributed brain networks including regions associated with lexical and combinatorial processing. 

In the appendix, we explored the features involved in the different recognition tasks. For example, in Figure 9 we show amplitude, phase and power differences associated with speech and non-speech segments; in Figure 8 we show a confusion matrix with color-coded consonants and vowels (phonemes) groups based on their motor (place of articulation) and acoustic (manner of articulation) features; in Figure 12 we show the frequency distribution of Part-Of-Speech (POS) categories which is most pronounced for function words (articles, pronouns, conjunctions) as compared to content words (nouns, adjectives, verbs).


**In regards to the issue of not yet publishing the BIDS data:**

We will release the BIDS data after the open ML competition associated with the dataset. Incidentally, it was a deliberate choice not to release the BIDS data for the competition. We did not want domain expertise to discourage participants without neuroscience backgrounds. By releasing serialised data, the data can be thought of as “just” tensors for machine learning. We were also concerned that the memory footprint of the dataset could become an obstacle. By serialising the data, we were also able to reduce the size of the dataset in memory from hundreds of GB to only about 50 GB. Finally, we needed more time to carefully pseudonymise the data for compliance with our research ethics approval.

summary.value: The authors introduce a new resource for the speech-decoding community. The dataset’s main contribution is its depth: more than 50 hours of 306-channel MEG data from a single volunteer listening to audiobooks. Crucially, it’s designed for immediate use by the machine-learning community. The data are available on Hugging Face and can be loaded with a simple, pip-installable library, and the authors provide baseline code and checkpoints to make their initial benchmark results for speech, phoneme, and word detection reproducible.

strengths_contributions.value: The main strength here is the “depth over breadth” approach. In a field where most non-invasive datasets offer only minutes of data per participant, having 50 hours from a single brain is a massive contribution that will enable new kinds of modeling. Since the train, validation, and test splits are all drawn from a contiguous story read by the same narrator, there’s a risk of linguistic context leaking across splits and inflating scores. summary.value: The authors present a publicly available MEG dataset along with a benchmark study focused on deep-individual-sampling recordings, from an individual subject. The dataset is preprocessed and structured to be readily usable for machine learning applications.

strengths_contributions.value:
Quality:
The approaches taken in data collection, preprocessing, and analysis are technically sound. The paper provides detailed documentation of the data acquisition process, standardization protocols, and sharing methodology. The claims made are well-supported by appropriate references. Notably, the authors are thorough in discussing the limitations of the dataset and clearly articulate its potential value to the research community.

Clarity:
The paper is well written, clearly structured, and easy to follow. It includes all the necessary components expected from a high-quality data release paper, including code for data processing and analysis. Additionally, the authors provide an API to facilitate access and usage of the dataset.

Originality/Significance:
The authors present and publicly release the largest naturalistic single-subject MEG dataset to date, involving approximately 50 hours of recording while the subject listens to audiobooks. This represents a significant advancement over the closest comparable effort as noted by the authors, which involved only 10 hours of data. The scale and design of the dataset offer promising opportunities for advancing BCI models and deepening our understanding of within-subject modeling.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
While the dataset is well-prepared for integration into machine learning pipelines, it is not currently BIDS-compliant, though the authors indicate plans for future compliance. Its current format appears tailored to the PNPL competition (Landau et al., 2025), which may hinder direct applicability in lab-specific workflows or broader neuroscience research settings.

Additionally, the limited scope of metadata release raises concerns. It remains unclear what concurrent data—beyond eye-tracking, cardiac activity, and articulatory movements—were collected or are available (e.g., behavioral annotations, demographic details), which could restrict the dataset’s utility for more comprehensive analyses.

Finally, as acknowledged by the authors, the use of a single-subject dataset inherently limits model generalizability across individuals, which constrains broader application and interpretation of findings.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: Instructions for fetching and organizing the dataset folders are insufficient, making it difficult to run the code without additional troubleshooting. Clearer documentation on data access and structure would be beneficial. Due to this lack of clarity, I was unable to test the code as intended.

additional_feedback.value: The repository does not indicate the Python version with which the code has been tested or is known to be compatible. Including this information would improve reproducibility and ease of integration into existing pipelines

final_justification.value: While some of my concerns were not fully addressed in the rebuttal, I still believe that the manuscript—describing the dataset created for the PNLP Challenge—serves as a helpful vehicle to promote its adoption and use by the broader community.

summary.value: The paper introduces LibriBrain, a new and significantly larger single-subject MEG-to-Speech dataset, which contains over 50 hours of data from a single participant—five times larger than the previously largest dataset of its kind. In addition, LibriBrain offers a range of open-source and reproducibility features, and establishes a publicly visible leaderboard to support deep learning competitions.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. This dataset offers a deeper MEG-to-Speech resource compared to previous datasets, which often lacked sufficient samples per subject. LibriBrain provides a novel dataset for the intersection of artificial intelligence and neuroscience, enabling exploration of large-scale model applications. Similar to how single-subject data abundance in fMRI-based visual decoding has led to improved performance, LibriBrain holds strong potential for further development and advances in MEG-based brain decoding research.

2. The dataset is fully open-source and can be accessed via a Python API. It also provides multiple options for data retrieval. By following the official tutorials, users can gain a comprehensive understanding of the dataset’s structure. Furthermore, the speech data is richly annotated, offering detailed labels across various dimensions.

3. The baseline benchmark provided with this dataset is intentionally simple, consisting of fundamental models commonly used in traditional speech tasks. This simplicity allows researchers to easily build upon it and explore more advanced architectures. Despite the basic benchmark, the experiments in the paper still demonstrate a clear relationship between data volume and decoding accuracy for the subject, exhibiting a certain scaling property. This aligns well with the current trend in large-scale model research.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. Although increasing the amount of data from a single subject can improve model performance, it is time-consuming and labor-intensive, which significantly limits the generalizability of models trained on this dataset. In real-world scenarios, collecting large-scale data from individual participants is often highly challenging—especially given the sensitive nature of the data and associated privacy concerns. Therefore, a crucial direction for future work is to expand the dataset to include multiple subjects, enabling the exploration of cross-subject generalization and shared neural representations.

2. From the perspective of model depth, the paper does not seem to explore how deeper or larger models could be leveraged to handle the increased scale of the LibriBrain dataset. Typically, if deeper models can better fit such large-scale data, it would suggest that MEG-to-Speech decoding also exhibits a scaling property with respect to model capacity. However, this work primarily focuses on validating the scaling behavior from the data size perspective, while overlooking the potential insights that could be gained from examining model complexity and depth.

3. In addition, the single-subject nature of the dataset also limits the application of foundation models. Such models typically rely on diverse, large-scale data from multiple subjects to learn generalized representations. The lack of inter-subject variability in LibriBrain constrains the ability to train or adapt foundation models effectively, which poses a challenge for advancing toward more universal MEG-to-Speech decoding systems.

summary.value: The authors release LibriBrain, a 50+ hour single-subject MEG speech listening dataset. The dataset is curated carefully and analyzed with respect to how it supports speech detection, phoneme classification, and word classification, with all tasks showing some benefit from increased data volume.

strengths_contributions.value:
**Quality**: Good. The dataset is prepared with high quality control and preprocessing (lengthy appendix describing preprocessing), accessible through a simple python library, and has predefined modeling splits. This dataset provides a good entrypoint for ML practicioners to engage with the area with minimal need to tangle with domain knowledge, while also adopting good practice for data preparation for neuroscientists.

**Clarity**: The work is tidily presented, in both figures and accompanying text. It is easy to understand how this work is situated compared to previous noninvasive brain-and-speech dataset releases and the importance of the increased data volume in one subject.

**Originality**: The listening experiment was designed to align with and extend past previous paradigms, which is appropriate for such a study. There is a clear distinction between this work and preceding works (Fig 1). 

**Significance**: This work provides good evidence for in-subject scaling, and also highlights the potential of stimulus averaging for enabling higher performance non-invasive decoding. It is likely that this work will be used frequently in future work in the area, and it seems intractable to collect any larger order of magnitude dataset within a single subject.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
**Quality**: While Figure 3 provides a straightforward overview, the subsequent Tables that show model performance against random baseline do not seem particularly informative. This is both because I would expect the random baseline to be a trivial baseline to outperform, and because it does not particularly touch on the nature of the dataset (you could produce the same analysis with any subset of the dataset). I would instead advocate e.g compressing these results and moving the supplemental analysis on the benefit of repeated stimuli to the main text.

**Significance**: I would appreciate some discussion of this work's implication for the outlook on single-subject scaling for the field. While scaling is encouraging, scaling across machine learning is most impactful when there is a clear runway for larger data collection. This does not appear to be the case for this domain. If the expectation is that cross-subject models will dominate future scaling efforts, is it most likely this dataset will serve as a rigorous test set? Alternatively, I would appreciate insight added to the supplement on the challenges of collecting this scale of single-subject data, and if the next order of magnitude of single-subject data could plausibly be justified.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

ethical_comments.value: No. The data was collected with standard consenting processes for the volunteer.

dataset_code_comments.value: Both data and code are available publicly with significant downloads already on the dataset. The code package for replicating reported experiments is simple. Small nitpick: It's unclear and undocumented why there are multiple scaling folders for the phoneme task.

additional_feedback.value:
- It seems plausibly worthwhile to provide some deeper view on the neural data in Figure 1, which only has a raw data view, compared to three statistical views of the audio.
- Many previous MEG datasets must inherently be occuring over a very short timescale. As LibriBrain proposes to scale to 50 hours, I see data was collected as far as two months apart, meaning the total dataset must span quite a while. Could the authors use their dataset to provide any characterization of whether MEG signals have day to day drift?
- It is mentioned several times that cross-subject performance is worse than single-subject performance while data-matched. It seems worthwhile to have a figure that supports this in the context of this dataset, since there are ~30-40 hours of other subjects listening to Sherlock Holmes.
- Section 4.3: Relatedly, for the claim, LibriBrain _scales_ better than Armeni 22 like-for-like - why? Is it due to the state of the art recording hardware, using single-subject data vs multi-subject data, subject variability in the particular evaluation subject, or preprocessing? Considering the gain between these two modes is just as substantial as the benefit from scaling from 10 to 50 hours. Further, Armeni 22 has at most 30 hours of data, according to Table 1. How does the Armeni model in 3C reach 50 hours?

final_justification.value:
The work is a clearly communicated and likely useful contribution. Having read the other reviews, I do not think there are major technical issues with the work. The authors did not particularly address my weaknesses or concerns, e.g.
- Having data have signal is already conveyed by the scaling plots, so the value of Table 3 (and beating random baseline) is still unclear to me.
- Lack of day-to-day drift in aggregate statistics does not imply signal stationarity. 
- While it's possible to collect 500 hours in a subject, I would have liked to hear a defense of how in-subject scaling would provide practical utility.

However, my concerns are mostly on the interpretation of the data and narrative of the work, which I do not think is a major issue for a dataset-track submission that already has an interested sub-community.

title.value: LibriBrain: Over 50 Hours of Within-Subject MEG to Improve Speech Decoding Methods at Scale

TLDR.value: LibriBrain is the largest non-invasive MEG dataset (over 50 hours) recorded from a single subject listening to naturalistic speech, designed to advance scalable and reproducible machine learning methods for speech decoding from brain activity.

abstract.value: LibriBrain represents the largest single-subject MEG dataset to date for speech decoding, with over 50 hours of recordings---5$\times$ larger than the next comparable dataset and 50$\times$ larger than most. This unprecedented `depth' of within-subject data enables exploration of neural representations at a scale previously unavailable with non-invasive methods. LibriBrain comprises high-quality MEG recordings together with detailed annotations from a single participant listening to naturalistic spoken English, covering nearly the full Sherlock Holmes canon. Designed to support advances in neural decoding, LibriBrain comes with a Python library for streamlined integration with deep learning frameworks, standard data splits for reproducibility, and baseline results for three foundational decoding tasks: speech detection, phoneme classification, and word classification. Baseline experiments demonstrate that increasing training data yields substantial improvements in decoding performance, highlighting the value of scaling up deep, within-subject datasets. By releasing this dataset, we aim to empower the research community to advance speech decoding methodologies and accelerate the development of safe, effective clinical brain-computer interfaces.

The PC Chairs will analyze aggregated data to understand how emerging technologies influence the research publication process. Please select all that apply below.
